The apex cryptocurrency traded at around $76,000, leaving it 0.6% above its 50-week simple moving average (SMA) of $75,580. The 50-week SMA is the average closing price of Bitcoin over the past 50 weeks, or around a year, and is typically viewed by traders as an indicator of the long-term trend. The slide began on Thursday when Bitcoin posted its biggest single-day loss since June, falling 5.5% from about $80,100 to $75,700. The selloff continued on Thursday, with the price hitting a low of $74,720. That briefly put it about 1.1% below average. Bitcoin recovered by the end of the session and closed back above the line at $75,800. Bitcoin has only just moved back above the average. It finished the week of September 20 at $81,150, Cointelegraph reported, citing TradingView data. At the time, the 50-week moving average was around $78,780. It was Bitcoin's first weekly close above the line since November 9, 2025. Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy, has been closely following the level. In a research note in August, he had said the 50-week average had served as a ceiling in past bear markets. In four out of the five bear markets that have ended, the first break above the bottom was the bottom. Galaxy also warned that the signal was not foolproof. Of 13 weekly crosses back above the average in past bear markets, two were followed by a lower low, both during the 2021-2022 downturn. Bitcoin closed above the line for seven weeks in a row as of the close of the week ended Nov. 1. That close was $78,220, or 3.3% above the average, according to Galaxy. Since then, the cushion has shrunk to well below 1%. At the time of writing, Bitcoin’s price was trading at $75,990, flat over the past 24 hours. title: NVIDIA Or Micron: Where Each Leads In The AI Buildout - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Investors buy both NVIDIA (NVDA) and Micron Technology (MU) to capture the spending on AI data centers: NVIDIA sells the computing systems, and Micron sells DRAM and NAND memory. Micron trades at 9.2 times earnings compared with 23.4 for NVIDIA, making it look like the cheaper way in. Yet NVIDIA said in August that soaring memory prices had prompted a reset of its gross margin expectations. So will memory prices keep rising, and can NVIDIA keep growing while it pays them? They are, although Micron expects the increases to slow. During its August 26, 2026 call, NVIDIA said memory price increases had exceeded its expectations and were headed even higher. For NVIDIA, that serves as a cost warning, but for Micron, those same prices are what it sells at. Micron provided a pricing outlook on its September 30 call. Management guided fiscal Q1 2027 revenue of $60 billion to $63 billion, compared with $54.2 billion in fiscal Q4 2026. That forecast assumes only single-digit growth in the bits of DRAM and NAND that Micron ships, leaving price and product mix to supply the rest of the rise. Management also said price increases would continue at a more moderate pace. Micron’s 86.0% guide for its gross margin sits just below the 86.8% it reported for fiscal Q4. So far it can, although its margin is slipping. NVIDIA guided fiscal Q3 2027 revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, compared with $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2. Management expects fiscal 2028 revenue to grow about 70% and said supply, including of its new Vera Rubin systems, would remain the bottleneck through at least the end of that year. The memory bill shows up in the margin instead. NVIDIA reported a 75.0% gross margin for fiscal Q2 and guided 74% for fiscal Q3, plus or minus half a point. Management expects it to bottom at 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4, then settle at 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028 as NVIDIA’s own price increases take effect. NVIDIA’s margins have also been far steadier than those of Micron. NVIDIA’s operating margin averaged 61.7% over the last three twelve-month periods, compared with 35.3% for Micron. Over those periods, NVIDIA’s twelve-month operating margin stayed between 58.1% and 65.2%, while Micron’s twelve-month operating margin climbed from 5.2% to 74.6% in two years. Over the latest twelve months, Micron comes out ahead on growth and margin. Micron’s revenue grew 256.3%, against 83.4% for NVIDIA. Its operating margin was 74.6%, compared with 65.2% for NVIDIA. Each company has debt under 1% of its market value. You cannot see from Micron’s low multiple how new its profits are. Micron’s quarterly operating margin was 45.0% in fiscal Q1 2026 and 80.7% by fiscal Q4. If memory prices fall, Micron stands to lose that margin, and its multiple would look less cheap on lower earnings. If NVIDIA’s growth stalls instead, you lose the growth its higher multiple pays for, as set out in a sales forecast that runs a full year ahead. Each stock has its own way to disappoint. A portfolio ready for a crash and a rally doesn’t need you to pick. Micron leads on its multiple, growth and margin over the latest twelve months, and memory prices are still rising. NVIDIA leads on how steady its margins have been, and its growth outlook holds even as memory costs pull its gross margin down. The memory prices behind Micron’s margin may rise more slowly from here, because Micron’s own management expects the increases to moderate. Micron’s gross margin for fiscal Q1 2027 is the number to watch when it reports in December 2026. If you own an S&P 500 or Nasdaq fund, you already own NVIDIA, alongside the same few giants that lead those funds. title: The S&P 500 Is Up 75% In 3 Years. Priced In Gold, It Is Down 14%. Which Is Real? - Trefis
content: Part of our series on building a mix that lasts. Start here: is 60/40 dead? Which is real? Both, and the gap between them is the interesting part. In dollars, your S&P 500 fund rose about three-quarters in three years. Measured against gold, it lost ground, because gold did even better. We’ll go stock by stock through the biggest names to see who really beat it. Here’s what the pros are actually working on, though: not which ruler is right, but what share of their money would hold its value if the dollar keeps losing ground to hard assets. We’ll come back to that, with a rule you can set this weekend. That stocks have had a great run. Our price data shows the S&P 500 fund SPY up 75.0% over three years, with dividends, from the close on November 6, 2023, to Friday’s close. What fewer people notice is that gold did better. Over the same three years, the gold fund GLD rose about 103%. Divide one by the other and the S&P 500, priced in ounces of gold, fell about 14%. Your bills are in dollars, so the dollar number is the one you live on. If your $100,000 became about $175,000, you can spend $175,000. That’s real. The gold number answers a different question: how much of that gain came from the companies, and how much from the dollar itself buying less? Gold doesn’t earn anything, and nobody can print more of it. When stocks beat gold, the businesses outran the currency. When gold beats stocks, part of what looked like growth was the measuring stick shrinking. Over the last three years, by this measure, the stick shrank faster than the average business grew. A simple way to see it on your own statement: take your balance three years ago and today, and divide each by the gold price on those dates. If the number of ounces went down, your money grew in dollars but lost ground against a hard asset. That doesn’t mean you lost money; your groceries are still priced in dollars. It means your plan has been quietly riding on the dollar. The index is an average, so we did the same sum for ten of its biggest companies. Here’s each one’s three-year return to Friday’s close, in dollars and priced in gold, on Trefis company data: Five of the ten beat gold. Apple and Meta trailed it slightly, and Amazon, Berkshire and Microsoft lost more ground. That’s a striking list. Two chip makers did most of the out-running, and both were hit hard on Thursday, when the AI trade unwound: chips and data-center builders fell hardest, after weeks of worry about power supply and growing opposition to new data centers. Nvidia closed at $181.60, down about 9% on the day, while SPY fell 4.4% to $733.00 and GLD rose 0.8%. We flagged power as the AI trade’s real risk on Nov 2, in Nvidia Stock’s Real Risk Isn’t China. It’s Power. And Microsoft, the third-largest U.S. company by market value, lost more than a fifth of its value in gold terms while its sales grew 18% over the past year. Strong businesses can still lose ground to a hard asset if you paid a high price for them. Three years is a short window, so we went back as far as our gold data goes, to November 2004. Here’s the S&P 500 fund priced in gold, with dividends, on month-end prices: Over 22 years they finished close. Along the way, each one beat the other by enormous margins for years at a time. In dollars, SPY grew about 9.3 times and GLD about 8.3 times over the period, roughly 10.7% and 10.1% a year. Gold beat stocks in 11 of the 21 full calendar years from 2005 to 2025. Close to a coin toss year to year, and a near tie over two decades. This is where gold earns its place, and where it costs you. Here’s the worst peak-to-bottom fall of each in the big selloffs, from daily prices with dividends, and when it got back to the old high: In the 2008 and 2020 crashes, gold fell less and recovered sooner; in 2022 both got back in December 2023. In its own slump, it took almost nine years to come back. On calendar years, gold rose 4.9% in 2008 while SPY fell 36.8%, and was roughly flat in 2022 while SPY fell 18.2%. Gold didn’t make money in every bad year. It just didn’t fall with stocks. The cost is the second row: from August 2011 to December 2015 gold lost almost half its value and didn’t recover until 2020, while SPY nearly doubled. It’s swinging hard right now too. GLD sat about 25% below its January high on Friday. Investors pulled $1.93 billion out of it in the month to Nov 4, about 1.4% of its assets. That’s the usual pattern: money chases gold after a big run (GLD rose about 64% in 2025) and leaves after a fall. Chasing it either way is the expensive part. 1. Measure your dollar bet. Add up what share of your portfolio would hold its value if the dollar kept losing ground to gold. For most people that’s close to zero: stocks, bonds and cash are all priced in dollars. Write the number down. 2. If you want a hedge, size it by rule. A small, fixed slice, say 5% to 10%, is enough to matter in a 2022 without sinking the plan in a 2013. In our test of mixes since 2017, a portfolio with 10% gold and 10% cash next to dividend stocks and the S&P 500 lost 6.2% in 2022, against 15.8% for 60/40. We break down what the gold and cash added in What If You Add Gold And Cash To A Dividend Portfolio? 3. Set a band and rebalance. For example: target 7%, trim above 9%, add below 5%. That way you sell some gold after runs like 2025 and buy some after falls like this year’s, without having to guess. What this replaces: piling into gold after a 64% year, or dumping it after a 25% drop. The risk: gold can go nearly a decade without paying you back, and a gold slice will lag in long stock rallies like 2013-2021. That’s why it’s a slice, not a strategy. We call it Cash is a guaranteed loss, and its cousin: every dollar asset carries a quiet bet on the dollar. Your stock gains are real, and you can spend them. But part of what looks like growth, in some years, is the ruler shrinking. A small hard-asset slice is how a long-run investor holds a position on that without having to predict it. content: Reports of an alleged Chinese intelligence asset (identified as Alice Huang/Huang Le, an executive at a regional customer entity) targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have generated significant headlines. Despite congressional inquiries and intense media coverage, Nvidia’s stock (NVDA) has remained relatively stable rather than suffering a major sell-off. Nvidia shares moved upward (~3%) due to several offsetting factors: Nvidia issued statements clarifying that interactions with overseas cloud customer representatives involved standard, non-sensitive business conversations with zero exposure of trade secrets or national security data. Both Nvidia and initial intelligence briefings indicate that the interaction did not result in a breach of classified information or core intellectual property. Nvidia stated that its interactions with the executive were standard business engagements typical for regional cloud customers. Nvidia’s AI chip architectures, trade secrets, and software stack (CUDA) are heavily partitioned and protected. Ordinary business or customer-facing communications do not expose sensitive national security secrets or technical schematics. Investors price semiconductor stocks primarily on underlying earnings power, revenue growth, and supply chain execution: Unprecedented AI Demand: Wall Street remains focused on the structural demand for Nvidia’s hardware across cloud service providers, enterprise software companies, and sovereign AI initiatives. Nvidia holds a dominant market share in high-performance AI accelerators. A personal or corporate espionage inquiry without operational disruption does not alter Nvidia’s competitive lead or revenue pipeline. The political reaction thus far points to administrative and export scrutiny rather than criminal action against Nvidia itself: While U.S. House committees have requested briefings to review cybersecurity protocols and export compliance, executive statements from U.S. leadership have framed Jensen Huang as an asset to American tech leadership rather than a target of enforcement. Washington’s primary lever against tech diversion to China remains export restrictions (e.g., bandwidth limits, performance caps) rather than targeting individual domestic technology firms. The intelligence concerns largely focus on foreign entities attempting to bypass U.S. export controls to acquire chips. Wall Street views attempts by foreign actors to illegally acquire Nvidia hardware as a broad regulatory risk affecting the entire semiconductor sector, rather than a structural flaw unique to Nvidia’s executive management

Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shareholders just lived through the roughest week for chip stocks in more than five years. On Thursday, the PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 12.25%, its biggest one-day drop since March 2020, as investors weighed what the new Congress could mean for data center construction. Nvidia fell 9.26% that day to $181.60. On Friday it bounced 2.78% to close at $186.64. Even after the bounce, Nvidia ended the week 8.8% lower and sits 22% below its record close of $239.24 on Oct. 6. Take a 64-year-old retiree who bought 1,000 shares on June 10, 2024, the day Nvidia’s 10-for-1 split took effect, at $121.79 a share. That was a $121,790 investment. At the October record the shares were worth $239,240. On Friday they were worth $186,640. They also hold $600,000 in other retirement savings and collect $2,500 a month from Social Security, so Nvidia is now 23.7% of a $786,640 portfolio. The question this weekend is whether Thursday was a warning to sell. The sell-off hit almost every chip name at once. The iShares Semiconductor ETF fell 12.15%, its worst day since March 2020, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF fell 11.21%. Micron fell 17.46% and Lam Research 16.36%. Nvidia’s 9.26% drop was one of the smaller ones. That gap matters. The stocks that fell hardest sell equipment and memory, which depend on what chipmakers and data center owners plan to spend next year. Nvidia sells into demand that exists today. Investors were pricing in a slowdown in future spending more than a drop in current orders. Friday brought some relief. Chip stocks rebounded across the board, and Nvidia traded as high as $194.90 during the day before settling at $186.64. Measured from the purchase, the investment is still well ahead. The 1,000 shares cost $121,790 and are worth $186,640, a gain of $64,850, or 53.2%, in under two and a half years. Measured from the peak, the shares have given back $52,600 in a month. Thursday alone took $18,530, and Friday returned $5,040 of it. Nvidia also pays more than it used to. It raised its quarterly dividend to 25 cents a share this year, from 1 cent. On 1,000 shares that is $1,000 a year, a yield of 0.54% at Friday’s price. The dividend is small next to the price swings, but it is a sign the company is generating more cash than it needs. The business is still growing at a pace few large companies have ever matched. Nvidia’s revenue over the past four reported quarters reached $302.97 billion, and its latest quarter’s revenue was up 105.9% from a year earlier. The stock is also cheaper than it looks after a run like this. At $186.64, Nvidia trades at about 23.6 times its earnings over the past year. Of the 62 analysts tracked, 59 rate it a buy or strong buy, and their average price target is $327.14, about 75% above Friday’s close. The next real test is close. Nvidia reports its quarterly results later this month, and that report will show whether customers are still ordering at the pace they were. The risk for this retiree is concentration. Nvidia is 23.7% of everything they own, and at the October peak it was 28.5%. A stock that can fall 9% in a day can fall 30% over a few months. A 30% drop from here would cost about $55,992, almost two years of the $30,000 a year Social Security pays them. Well-known skeptics are still betting against the sector. Michael Burry disclosed this week that he took profits on a quarter of his bet against the VanEck Semiconductor ETF after Thursday’s plunge, and said the rest of the position remains very large. Selling part of the position is a reasonable option. If the retiree sells 300 of the 1,000 shares at Friday’s price: If the shares sit in a traditional IRA, the sale itself creates no tax bill today. Trimming keeps most of the upside if the analysts are right and the next report is strong. It also moves some of a paper gain into cash before the report, when the stock is likely to swing again. No one knows whether Thursday was the start of a longer slide or a sharp one-day scare. The analyst targets were mostly set before this week. And the $2,918 tax figure assumes the retiree’s income keeps them in the 15% long-term capital gains bracket; a larger sale could push part of the gain higher. A 64-year-old who turned $121,790 into $186,640 with Nvidia is still well ahead, even after losing $18,530 on the chip sector’s worst day since 2020. The bigger question is whether 23.7% of a retirement should ride on one stock heading into its next earnings report. title: NVDA Stock Rebounds 4% but $180 Support Remains Critical After Midterm Selloff for Nvidia - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia shares extended their decline from record highs above $243, falling towards $181 before recovering 4% on Friday, as Democratic midterm victories, rising infrastructure costs, electricity constraints and growing opposition to data-centre expansion intensified concerns about the semiconductor industry’s growth prospects. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares dropped below $200 on Thursday, falling towards $181 and extending their retreat from record highs above $243. The stock attempted a recovery on Friday, gaining approximately 4%, but buyers failed to push it back above the psychological $200 level, leaving shares close to the important $180 support zone. The latest weakness reflects growing concerns about the enormous infrastructure commitments underpinning semiconductor valuations. Investors are increasingly questioning whether major technology companies can maintain their current investment pace as financing costs rise, electricity availability becomes more challenging and political resistance to new data-centre developments gains momentum. The Democratic victories in the US midterm elections have introduced another challenge for Nvidia and the broader semiconductor industry. Gina Hinojosa’s victory in Texas, alongside political changes in Ohio and Georgia involving Amy Acton and Keisha Lance Bottoms, has strengthened opposition to unchecked data-centre expansion. Proposals for restrictions and freezes on new developments highlight growing concerns about electricity consumption, water requirements and rising utility bills. Reports that 40 of 41 direct votes concerning data-centre projects failed further illustrate the changing public sentiment. For Nvidia, the implications could extend beyond political headlines. Delays in construction, additional regulatory requirements and higher infrastructure expenses could affect the spending plans of major cloud providers, which remain among the company’s most important customers. Electricity availability is becoming a significant bottleneck for the infrastructure industry. Technology companies may increasingly need to finance additional power generation and grid improvements rather than relying entirely on existing electricity networks. Financing conditions are also creating pressure. CoreWeave has faced growing scrutiny as yields on some of its debt maturing in 2032 approached 15%, highlighting the risks associated with heavily leveraged infrastructure expansion. Amazon has reportedly experienced delays involving Nvidia-equipped server racks waiting in warehouses because certain data centres lack sufficient electricity to operate them. These developments raise questions about construction schedules, capital efficiency and whether the enormous investments being made will generate sufficient returns. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $180 today where NVDA is testing the last support at the 100 weekly SMA in green. The trend will depend on whether the 100 SMA holds as support. Despite the share-price weakness, Nvidia continues strengthening its position across the semiconductor supply chain. CEO Jensen Huang reportedly consulted with Marvell Technology and Lumentum executives ahead of Marvell’s approximately $115 billion enterprise-value acquisition of Lumentum. Nvidia previously invested $2 billion in each company, increasing its exposure to optical networking and connectivity technologies required for expanding data-centre infrastructure. However, the transaction also highlights the enormous capital requirements associated with building the next generation of computing infrastructure. Demand for computing capacity remains substantial. Anthropic reportedly plans to increase its computing capacity beyond 3.5 gigawatts by the end of 2026, potentially reaching approximately 7 gigawatts in 2027. Samsung Electronics is also preparing to manufacture base dies for high-bandwidth memory chips intended for Nvidia and AMD, with mass production targeted for 2030. However, Nvidia is facing increasing competition from custom processors. Google and Oracle plan to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027, providing customers with another alternative to Nvidia-powered systems. Although Nvidia retains considerable advantages through its software ecosystem, performance and established customer relationships, expanding competition could eventually put pressure on pricing and market share. The technical picture has deteriorated significantly following the decline below $200. Friday’s 4% rebound provides some relief, but buyers have yet to reclaim this important psychological level. The immediate focus remains on $180 support. A sustained break below this area could expose further downside towards $150, while a recovery above $200 would be needed to improve the short-term outlook. Nvidia remains a major semiconductor player with substantial exposure to long-term computing demand. Nevertheless, investors are increasingly questioning whether infrastructure spending can continue at its previous pace. For now, sellers retain control of the technical picture, while political opposition, electricity shortages, financing risks and growing competition could keep Nvidia shares under pressure.

Taiwan Semiconductor, the world's largest chip foundry, is considering expanding its business into advanced storage chip manufacturing and has, at the request of its largest customer NVIDIA, begun formulating plans to produce 3D DRAM (three-dimensional dynamic random-access memory). The Zhitong Finance APP has learned that, according to media reports, Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM.US), the world's largest chip foundry, is considering expanding its business into advanced storage chip manufacturing and has, at the request of its largest customer NVIDIA (NVDA.US), begun formulating plans to produce 3D DRAM (three-dimensional dynamic random-access memory). If this plan is ultimately implemented, Taiwan Semiconductor could further expand its influence in the artificial intelligence (AI) hardware supply chain. According to media reports citing two insiders, Taiwan Semiconductor has recently begun studying production plans for 3D DRAM. This move stems from NVIDIA's demand for advanced memory chips and reflects that AI chip designers are actively seeking to diversify their sources of critical components. 3D DRAM is an advanced memory chip technology that employs a three-dimensional architecture, aiming to increase storage density through novel cell layouts and manufacturing processes, while providing more technological options for future high-performance computing systems. For Taiwan Semiconductor, which has long focused on logic chip foundry and advanced packaging, entering advanced DRAM manufacturing would mean further expanding its business portfolio. Currently, Taiwan Semiconductor dominates the global advanced logic chip manufacturing sector and is also a key manufacturing partner for NVIDIA's AI accelerators. If it further enters the advanced memory chip production field in the future, Taiwan Semiconductor will have the opportunity to play a role in more critical segments of AI computing hardware. This potential business expansion comes at a time when the global memory chip market is facing severe supply constraints. As the boom in generative AI and data center construction continues, demand for high-performance computing hardware and associated memory chips is surging, tightening supply and driving prices sharply higher. For AI chip designers such as NVIDIA, memory chips are a critical component that determines the performance and production scale of computing systems. Supply shortages could not only drive up hardware manufacturing costs but also constrain the pace of AI infrastructure deployment. Consequently, major tech companies, including NVIDIA and Apple (AAPL.US), are actively seeking additional sources of memory chip supply to mitigate supply chain risks. The impact of rising storage chip prices has also begun to ripple through the consumer electronics market. Earlier this year, Apple raised the prices of some products, citing higher storage costs, highlighting that the tight supply of storage chips is no longer confined to the AI server sector but is affecting a broader range of electronic product markets. Against this backdrop, NVIDIA is urging Taiwan Semiconductor to research 3D DRAM production, which may help it establish a more diversified advanced storage chip supply system in the future. However, the relevant plans are currently still in the preliminary research and planning stages. The report did not disclose the scale of funding Taiwan Semiconductor plans to invest, its potential production capacity, the mass-production timeline, or whether it will formally launch commercial production in the future. Furthermore, 3D DRAM is not entirely the same technological route as High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), which is widely used in current AI accelerators, and Taiwan Semiconductor's research into 3D DRAM production does not mean it has decided to enter the existing HBM market. title: What Sent NVIDIA Stock Lower? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. NVIDIA (NVDA) stock fell 9.3% on Thursday, November 5, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 4.4% in the same session. The company issued no announcement, earnings report or filing. The stock fell as part of a sell-off of AI chip stocks that day. So what set off the sell-off, and why did NVIDIA get caught in it? Chip stocks fell across the board on November 5 amid post-election fears of a data center slowdown. Qualcomm declined after issuing a light outlook with its quarterly results, and NVIDIA slid with the other AI chip stocks. That fear matters for NVIDIA because most of its sales come from data centers. Management said on an August 26, 2026 call that data center revenue accounted for $89 billion of the company’s $96 billion in total revenue during its fiscal second quarter of 2027, which ended July 26, 2026. On the same call, management said capital spending by the top five hyperscalers, the largest cloud companies, was expected to reach nearly $800 billion in 2026. A slowdown in that spending is the risk the sell-off priced in. No. All five companies on NVIDIA’s Trefis peer list fell further during that session. Qualcomm lost 9.5% and Advanced Micro Devices lost 17.3%, while Intel, Broadcom and Marvell Technology fell by amounts in between. The technology sector and the wider market fell less. XLK, the fund that tracks the Information Technology sector, lost 8.0%, and the Nasdaq Composite index lost 5.5%. NVIDIA moved with its group: the stock fell more than the technology sector fund, but less than every one of its peers. Days like this are rare. Here’s what happened the last 21 times. NVIDIA stock had not seen a fall this large in any session over the prior 365 days. The drop also came at the end of a month-long slide. From October 7 to November 5, the stock lost 23.5%, against a 5.7% fall for the S&P 500. That slide followed the stock’s 52-week closing high of $239.24 on October 6, 2026; its 52-week closing low was $165.17 on March 30, 2026. Over twelve months, NVIDIA stock has lost 8.4%, while the S&P 500 returned 9.9%. At the November 5 close, after the fall, the stock still traded at 14.5 times its sales over the past twelve months, against 3.2 times for the S&P 500. NVIDIA is expected to report results for its fiscal third quarter of 2027 later in November 2026, and its data center revenue is the figure to watch. title: What’s Going To Happen With NVIDIA Stock Soon? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. NVIDIA (NVDA) stock fell 9.3% on November 5, 2026, marking its largest one-day drop in a year. Shareholders also face a strain management has already acknowledged. During its August 26, 2026 call, management said NVIDIA’s gross margin would get worse before it got better. Below are the reports and events most likely to move NVIDIA stock over the next six months. NVIDIA is expected to report its fiscal Q3 2027 results on November 17, 2026. This will be the company’s first report since that August call. Management guided revenue to $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, compared with $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2 2027. The guide counts no data center sales to China. Management left those sales out of its outlook because of geopolitical uncertainty. In fiscal Q2 2027, NVIDIA’s shipments of Hopper 200 products to customers in China came to less than 1% of its data center revenue. Revenue against that guide is the figure to watch in November 2026. NVIDIA expects its gross margin to dip because of memory. Management said in August 2026 that memory prices had risen more than it expected and were still heading higher. Management guided gross margin to a low of 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4 2027, down from 75% in fiscal Q2 2027. For fiscal Q3 2027, it guided gross margin to 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points. The drop matters at NVIDIA’s size. Each point of gross margin on its $303 billion of revenue over the past twelve months is worth about $3 billion a year. Management expects the margin to edge back up in fiscal 2028, as price increases NVIDIA has already set take effect. The gross margin NVIDIA reports for fiscal Q4 2027 is the figure to watch, with results expected in February 2027. NVIDIA began production shipments of Vera Rubin, the platform that follows Blackwell, in August 2026. Purchase orders are already in from every major hyperscaler. Management expected Vera Rubin to make up about 20% of data center revenue in fiscal Q3 2027. Data center revenue as a whole was $89 billion in fiscal Q2 2027. NVIDIA also expects growth in sales to hyperscalers, the largest cloud companies, to pick up again in fiscal Q4 2027 as Vera Rubin supply grows. For now, management expects growth to come mainly from its NeoCloud, industrial and enterprise customers. The limit is supply rather than orders. Management expects supply to remain a bottleneck at least through the end of fiscal 2028. Growth in NVIDIA’s sales to hyperscalers is the measure to watch when it reports in February 2027. Owning the stock through these reports means being ready for a fall like the one it has just taken. The stock dropped 24.1% from its October 6, 2026 close to November 5, marking the largest drop of the past year. That fall took 22 trading sessions and came before either report. Rattled by November 5? It has happened 21 times before. Here’s what came next. If a second fall of that size would push you to sell, the holding is larger than you can carry through the November 2026 and February 2027 reports. title: Will Nvidia Stock Jump 20% In The Next 30 Days? - Trefis
content: Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. Could Nvidia jump 20% in the next 30 days? Yes, it could, and it has done it many times before. We’ll give you the real odds, the numbers behind the business, the dated catalyst and how far it has fallen before. But here’s the number the pros reach for first after a day like Thursday: not where Nvidia trades in December, but how much of it they already own, counting the Nvidia hiding inside their index funds. We’ll come back to it at the end. Nvidia closed Thursday at about $181.60, down about 9.3% from Wednesday’s $200.13. That came on a rough day for everything: the S&P 500 fund SPY fell 4.4% to $733.00 and the Nasdaq-100 fund QQQ 6.5%. The chip makers fell harder still: Broadcom lost about 10% and the chip fund SMH about 11%. It was the AI trade unwinding: the chip makers and the companies building the power and data centers behind AI fell hardest. The worry has been building for weeks. Power is the bottleneck, opposition to new data centers is growing town by town, and the new Congress can lean on both; a Wall Street Journal article argued on Thursday that the backlash could play into the hands of Big Tech. We flagged power as the AI trade’s real risk on Nov 2, in “Nvidia Stock’s Real Risk Isn’t China. It’s Power.” Nvidia had held up earlier in the week while the data-center builders fell hard; whether it is now the dip to buy is the question in should you buy Nvidia stock at $182? Here’s the straight answer from Nvidia’s own history. We looked at every 30-day stretch (21 trading days) in the Trefis price cache and counted how often the stock ended at least 20% higher, or at least 20% lower: A 20% month for Nvidia is uncommon, not rare: roughly 1 in 7 or 8, and about 1 in 6 after a big down day. Those stretches overlap, so treat them as a feel for the odds, not a forecast. The closer match is the last row. Thirty days after Nvidia’s 44 earlier days of 7%+ falls since 2010, it was higher 23 times and lower 21, with a median gain of about 4%. The big rebounds came mostly after the March 2020 crash and the late-2022 bottom; two of the four further 20% falls came in late 2018. So the honest answer: a 20% jump is possible, it has happened after big drops before, and a month after a big down day Nvidia has been close to a coin flip. A 20% jump from about $181.60 gets you to about $218. That’s not a new high. Nvidia closed at $217.94 just seven trading days earlier, on October 27. So the upside case isn’t a moonshot; it’s a return to late October. Whether that’s a fair price depends on the business, and here the numbers are striking: After Thursday, Nvidia trades at about the market’s average multiple, for a company growing sales more than 80% a year. That’s the upside case in one line. The stock went nowhere for a year while the business kept compounding, so the multiple came down; Thursday alone took it from about 25 times earnings at Wednesday’s close to about 23. The other side of the same line: a market that pays an average multiple for 83% growth is telling you it doubts the growth lasts. That doubt is exactly the power and data-center question above. Next to its peers, Nvidia looks neither cheapest nor most expensive, but it has the widest margins of the big designers, Micron’s memory-cycle peak aside: P/E at Thursday’s close; sales growth and margin over the past 12 months. Micron’s low multiple is the warning label on the whole group: memory makers earn their biggest profits at the top of a cycle, and investors price that in. The dated catalyst for Nvidia is its quarterly report: Nvidia’s notice lists Tuesday, Nov 17, after the close. That report, and what the big buyers say about next year’s data-center spending, will move the stock more than anything we can measure now. This belongs right next to the upside case. Here are Nvidia’s biggest falls, measured on dividend-adjusted closes, with how long it took to get back to the old high: Nvidia has lost more than half its value three times since 2007. Once it took more than seven years to get back. The 2018 fall took less than three months to hit bottom and about 14 months more to recover. The 2022 fall went on for almost eleven months, then recovered in about seven. In 2020 and 2022, Nvidia fell harder than SPY and still got back to its old high months before SPY did. The 2008 case is the exception worth remembering: a 2007 buyer waited until 2016. Put those next to today. From the October 6 high of $239.24, a 2020-size fall would mean about $148, a 2018-size fall about $105, and a 2022-size fall about $81. We’re not saying any of those will happen. We’re saying a long-run Nvidia owner has lived through each of them, and your plan should be able to as well. Here’s what’s less random than the next 30 days: how much of your money rides on this one stock. If you own an S&P 500 fund, you own Nvidia whether you bought it or not. Nvidia is 7.30% of SPY, its second-largest holding after Apple. Say you have $1 million, with 70% in an S&P 500 fund and no Nvidia shares at all. You still own about $51,000 of Nvidia, 5.1% of everything. Buy another 5% directly on the dip and you’re at about 10%, and Thursday’s fall alone would have cost you about $9,400 on it. That number is something you can find this weekend and act on. The 30-day move isn’t. And it’s not just Nvidia. Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta, the companies buying Nvidia’s chips, plus Broadcom, add up to about 19% more of SPY. Together with Nvidia that’s roughly 26.5% of the fund riding on one spending boom. Three steps, none of which needs a guess about December. 1. Add up your total Nvidia. Direct shares, plus your S&P 500 fund times 7.30%, plus any Nasdaq-100 or chip fund times its Nvidia weight (about 8% in QQQ and about 20% in SMH in late October). Write down one number, as a share of your portfolio. 2. Set your band before Nov 17. Pick the most you’d want in one stock, say 8% to 10% of your portfolio, and the level that makes you trim, say 12%. If you’re under the band and you believe in the business, add in pieces. If you’re over it, trim back to the band, whatever the price did. 3. Decide what you do after a 2022-size fall. If Nvidia went to about $81, would you buy, hold or sell? Whatever the answer, write it down now, while you’re not looking at a red screen. What this replaces: buying a big chunk on Friday morning because a 20% bounce feels likely, or selling because Thursday hurt. The risk: if Nvidia jumps 20% and you were under your band, you’ll own less of the jump. That’s the price of a plan that also works if it falls another third. A 20% month is a 1-in-7 shot; your exposure is a number. Since 2016, Nvidia rose 20% or more in about 13% of 30-day stretches. After Thursday it trades near the market’s multiple, about 23 times earnings against about 22 for the S&P 500, with sales up 83% and $127 billion of free cash flow, and it has fallen 56% and 66% in the past eight years. Nvidia is 7.30% of SPY, so most investors own more than they think. Add up your total, set a band before the Nov 17 report, and decide now what you’d do after a 2022-size fall. title: The Nasdaq Fell 5% In A Day. What Happened The Last 21 Times? - Trefis
content: Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. The past can’t tell you what Friday does. It can tell you something more useful: whether a plan that holds through days like this has paid off before. We’ll come back to that at the end. Thursday was a rough one. Using the big index funds as stand-ins, the S&P 500 (SPY) fell 4.4% to $733.00 and the Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) 6.5%. The Dow fund and the small-company fund fell less than the Nasdaq, while gold (GLD) and long Treasuries (TLT) edged up. It was the AI trade unwinding: the chip makers and the companies building the power and data centers behind AI fell hardest. The worry has been building for weeks. Power is the bottleneck, opposition to new data centers is growing town by town, and the new Congress can lean on both; on Wednesday, Meta’s president told a Wall Street Journal conference that the midterm results will make building data centers harder. We flagged power as the AI trade’s real risk on Nov 2, in Nvidia Stock’s Real Risk Isn’t China. It’s Power. The damage came from the very top of the market. Ten of the biggest names we track lost roughly $1.5 trillion of market value between them in one session: Nvidia alone lost about as much value as Apple, Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft combined. The chip makers lost the most, and the companies that buy their chips lost far less; we take that split apart in Is The AI Trade Officially In Trouble? So here’s the question nearly everyone has after Thursday: is the market overreacting? Nobody can tell you what Friday does. But we can tell you what happened every other time it looked like this. We went through every trading day in the Trefis price cache from December 31, 2002 to November 4, 2026 and kept the days when the S&P 500 fell at least 3.5% and the Nasdaq Composite fell at least 5%. There were 21. Thursday, with the S&P 500 down 4.4% and the Nasdaq Composite down 5.5%, is the 22nd. Days like Thursday travel in packs. Eleven of the 21 came in one stretch, the 2008-09 crisis. A 5% Nasdaq day is rarely alone. In the fall of 2008 there were ten of them in about nine weeks. In March 2020 there were three in eight days. One of the 21 landed on November 5, 2008, the day after a presidential election. Thursday came two days after this year’s midterms. Here’s the S&P 500 after all 21 days, price only, no dividends: The next week and the next three months were close to a coin flip. The next year and the next five were not. A week later the range ran from a further double-digit fall (after March 9, 2020) to a double-digit gain (after November 20, 2008). That’s noise, not a pattern you can trade. Three months later the worst case came after September 29, 2008, with more of that crisis still ahead. Then the picture changes. A year later the index was higher 20 times out of 21, with a median gain of 27%. The one miss was that same September 29, 2008 day, a bit lower a year on. Five years later, for the 18 days old enough to measure, it was higher every time, roughly doubling at the median. Price only: dividends would add to every line. The 2022 and 2025 days aren’t five years old yet, so the five-year row covers 18 days. The days overlap (ten in fall 2008), so this is really five or six episodes, not 21 independent tests. The window starts on December 31, 2002, after the 2000-2002 dot-com fall, so that bear market is not in this data set. Thursday’s figures are the SPY and QQQ funds; the precedents use the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite indexes. A median hides the hard part, so here it is. In each of the last three bear markets, here’s how far the funds and the market’s biggest AI name fell from peak to bottom, and how many months it took to get back to the old high from the bottom, on dividend-adjusted daily prices: Every one of these came all the way back. Some took months, and 2008 took years. Thursday’s drop is small next to any of those rows. Nvidia ended the day about a quarter below its high, against a two-thirds fall in 2022. That doesn’t mean it can’t go lower. It means the history in our first two tables already includes falls far worse than Thursday, and the year-later numbers still came out the way they did. Here’s the honest answer: the data can’t say about this week, and neither can anyone else. What it can say is which question has an answer. “Will it bounce Friday?” had a coin-flip answer 21 times. “Will I be glad I held on a year from now?” had a nearly one-sided answer 21 times. We wrote earlier this week about whether this Nasdaq selloff looks more like 2000 or 2018; that’s the piece to read if your worry is the AI trade itself rather than the market. “We live in decades. Why worry about the next ten minutes like a fruit fly?” – Anonymous Make a plan for the next three months, not a trade for Monday. Three steps: 1. Assume there may be more days like this. In 2008 and 2020 they came in clusters. A week after two of the 21 days the index was already 10% or more lower again. Decide now what you’d do if SPY fell another 10%, to about $660. Write it down. 2. Rebalance by rule, not by mood. If your stocks have drifted well below your target share, a pre-set band tells you when to buy back to it. If they haven’t, you do nothing, and that’s a decision too. 3. Check your chip exposure. Thursday’s biggest falls were in chips. An S&P 500 fund already holds Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD and Micron; Nvidia and Broadcom alone are about a tenth of SPY. Count them before adding more. The risk: the worst three-month case in the data was another 21% fall. A plan doesn’t prevent that; it means you’ve already decided what you do inside it. What it replaces: selling after a 5% day, or buying everything at once because “it always bounces.” It didn’t always bounce within a week. What to watch: whether more 5% days follow in a cluster, and Nvidia’s quarterly report later this month. Both are reasons to check your plan, not to trade. We call it Plan, don’t react. The scariest day in a year is rarely the one that decides the year. Of the 21 days like Thursday since 2002, the one that hurt most a year later came in the thick of the 2008 crisis, and even it was 53% higher five years on. The short run is loud. The long run, in this data, was kinder. History says Thursday’s drop told you little about next week and a lot about how to plan. After the 21 earlier days like it, the S&P 500 was higher a week later only 10 times and three months later 12 times, but a year later 20 times, median +27% (price only). The bear markets around them took SPY 5 to 41 months to recover. Plan for more rough days, rebalance by rule, and judge this by where you’ll be in a year, not on Friday. Follow this story with us: if more days like Thursday come, we’ll add them to the table and show what changed. The next three months may be rough; your plan doesn’t have to be. title: Is The AI Trade Officially In Trouble? - Trefis
content: Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. Short answer: a day like Thursday isn’t trouble. Trouble has a definition, and it’s simple: the four big buyers of AI chips cutting what they plan to spend in 2027. Until that happens, a 9% day is a price story, not a business story. The question that will still matter next year is a quieter one: how much of your money rides on AI, counting your index fund too? We’ll come back to it. That it was an ugly day. SPY fell 4.4% and QQQ 6.5%. It was the AI trade unwinding: the chip makers and the companies building the power and data centers behind AI fell hardest. Power is the bottleneck, opposition to new data centers is growing town by town, and the new Congress can lean on both; a Wall Street Journal article argued on Thursday that the backlash could play into the hands of Big Tech. We flagged it on Nov 2, in “Nvidia Stock’s Real Risk Isn’t China. It’s Power.” The AI trade has two sides: the companies that sell the build-out (chips, power gear, cooling) and the four that pay for it. Thursday split them cleanly: The sellers fell about 12% on average; the buyers about 3%. In dollars, the sellers lost roughly $940 billion of market value and the buyers about $350 billion. Look at the last column. The hardest falls came where the biggest gains had been: Micron had more than tripled in a year and AMD had nearly doubled. Nvidia, the face of the trade, was flat over the 12 months even before Thursday. And Vertiv now sits about half below its high. On Wednesday the market paid the buyers for spending less: they rose while Nvidia fell 3.2%. We wrote up that trade in why Amazon and Google stock rose. On Thursday nobody got paid; the buyers just fell far less. Put the two days together and Nvidia is down about 12% from Tuesday’s close, while the four buyers, on average, are up about 1%. That’s investors betting that if spending slows, the suppliers get hurt and the buyers keep the cash. It’s a guess about the future, priced in two days. It isn’t news about the businesses: the latest spending plans are still the ones the four gave with their results in late October. So let’s look at the businesses. Here’s the classic Trefis check on all eleven: what you pay, how fast sales are growing, and whether profit margins are holding. P/E is at Thursday’s close; growth and margins are over the last 12 reported months. All eleven are growing. Of the ten with five years of history, nine earn margins at or above their five-year average; Meta is the exception, and only by two points. That isn’t what a business in trouble looks like. A few things stand out. Nvidia traded at about 25 times earnings before Thursday and about 23 after, less than Microsoft, while growing sales several times faster. Micron, at about 9 times, is priced as if its margins won’t last: they’re running at more than three times its five-year average. AMD, at nearly 90 times, is the one priced for a lot to go right. The risk in these stocks is the price you pay for growth that has to keep coming, not growth that has stopped. This is the real question under the AI trade, because the buyers’ spending is the sellers’ revenue. Here’s their capital spending story in one table: The four plan to spend more this year than their businesses brought in over the past year. In that year they kept about $61 billion of free cash between them. Nvidia alone kept $127 billion. That last line is the whole story. The money hasn’t vanished; it has moved down the chain, from the buyers’ cash flow to the sellers’ profits. For scale, the seven sellers in our table took in about $660 billion of revenue over the past year, less than the four buyers plan to spend in 2026. Not every capex dollar lands with these seven, but it shows who depends on whom. And the buyers say they aren’t done. Alphabet has said its spending will rise “significantly” in 2027 and Amazon “meaningfully”; Microsoft says it expects to stay free-cash-flow positive while it builds. Amazon is the one already spending more cash than it makes. There’s a twist, too. If towns and states slow new data centers, the capacity that’s already built gets scarcer, and the four buyers own a great deal of it. A pause can hurt the builders and help the incumbents at the same time. One thing: the buyers spending less on AI next year than they said. If two or more of the four hold 2027 spending flat or cut it, the build-out is slowing, and that’s the moment to revisit your plan. Two dates bring real data: Nvidia reports its quarter on Nov 17, and the four buyers report in late January and early February, with their 2027 plans. A second, earlier tell sits in the tables above: if the buyers’ revenue growth slows while their spending keeps climbing, their free cash flow shrinks further, and pressure to cut rises. A red Thursday isn’t either of those. Lower than this, even with the business fine. Here’s how far each fell in the 2022 bear market, how many months it took to get back to its old high from the bottom, and the 2008 fall for those old enough: In 2022 the buyers kept spending, and Nvidia still lost two-thirds of its value. Thursday left it about a quarter below its high. That’s the honest frame for a day like Thursday. A price can fall much further than this without anything breaking in the business, and it can take a year or more to come back. Which is why the plan below is about size, not prediction. “A falling price tells you how other people feel. The business tells you what it is worth.” – Anonymous 1. Count your AI, all of it. Your direct shares, plus what’s inside your index funds, plus the builders and power names that ride the same spending. Nvidia, Broadcom and the four buyers alone are about a quarter of an S&P 500 fund. Most people who count this way find more than they thought; we show how in how much AI you really own. 2. Set a band, not a target. Pick the share you want in AI, then a range around it. For example, a 25% target with a band of 20% to 30%. Above 30%, trim. Below 20%, add. Inside the band, do nothing. 3. Let the band decide, not the day. The move this replaces is selling after a 9% chip day, or buying everything on the dip. If Thursday pushed your count below the band, the rule says add, at prices you already decided were fair. If you’re still above it after Thursday, you were too heavy before Thursday. The risk: if this turns into a 2022-style fall, a band still loses money. You’ll buy on the way down and the price can keep falling, as the table above shows. What the band does is cap how much of your money is exposed, so the loss is one you planned for. Two ideas, really. Exposure hides in plain sight: your index fund owned every side of Thursday’s trade, the sellers and the buyers. And price isn’t the business: a day like Thursday for AMD tells you how other investors felt that day; the buyers’ 2027 plans and their cash flow will tell you what the business is worth. Watch the plans, size by the band, and let the price do what prices do. The AI trade isn’t officially in trouble; it’s officially volatile. The sellers fell about four times as much as the buyers on Thursday, yet all eleven are growing revenue and nine of ten are running at or above their five-year margins. The buyers plan about $730 billion of 2026 capex, and Alphabet and Amazon have said 2027 goes higher. Trouble is two or more of the four holding 2027 spending flat or lower, which you’ll see in late January. Until then, count your total AI exposure, set a band, and rebalance only when the count crosses it. Follow this story with us: we’ll be back after Nvidia’s report and again when the buyers set their 2027 plans, with what changed and what didn’t. Thursday tests the plan, not the trade. title: Should You Buy Nvidia Stock At $182? - Trefis
content: Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. Democrats won both chambers on Tuesday, and Texas elected a governor who has called for a pause on new data centers. On Wednesday the market treated that as a brake on AI building. The stocks that power and cool data centers fell hardest: Vertiv −12.9%, Vistra −13.8%, Eaton −9.9%, GE Vernova −9.3%. The companies that pay for the buildings rose: Microsoft +6.7%, Amazon +6.1%, Alphabet +3.2%, Meta +1.4%. Nvidia, which sells them the chips, closed at $200.13, down 3.2%. On Thursday Nvidia fell another 9.3%, to $181.60. On Wednesday alone the gap between the buyers and their supplier was about 7.5 points. The four buyers rose 4.4% on average, equal-weighted, while Nvidia fell 3.2%. That’s the trade in one line: less building means more cash for the buyers and less revenue for the seller. It only works if the building actually slows. Broadcom −2.0%, CoreWeave −9.9%, Constellation Energy −6.7%; AMD rose 1.0% after its record-quarter report on Tuesday. Nvidia had already fallen 7.1% over five days and 16% over a month by Wednesday’s close, on doubts about whether AI spending pays off, doubts that are older than the vote. That it is cheaper than the companies that buy from it, on the cash it actually makes: The four biggest buyers made about $61 billion of free cash together. Nvidia made about $127 billion by itself. That isn’t a coincidence. The buyers’ capital spending is a large part of Nvidia’s revenue, which grew 83% over the last year to about $303 billion, with an operating margin of 65%. So when investors cheer “less capex” at Amazon or Alphabet, they’re also cheering less revenue at Nvidia. Nvidia trades at about 23 times its last year’s earnings, below Microsoft and well below Broadcom and AMD. Free cash flow is each company’s free-cash-flow margin times its revenue over the last twelve reported months, from Trefis market data: Nvidia 41.9% of $303.0B; Microsoft 17.3% of $346.4B; Meta 11.9% of $241.6B; Alphabet 4.2% of $471.1B; Amazon −5.9% of $797.5B; Broadcom 44.2% of $89.1B; AMD 15.5% of $45.4B. The four buyers total about $61B. At Thursday’s close, Nvidia’s free cash flow trades at about 35 times, a 2.9% yield. Not easily, and not first. Each of the four is spending because it fears falling behind the other three; whoever cuts first hands the others its customers. We laid out that trap in why Big Tech can’t stop spending on AI. Their own words point the same way: Alphabet says its spending will rise “significantly” in 2027 and Amazon “meaningfully”. A state pause in Texas moves a data center to another state; it doesn’t cancel the chips inside it. So the question isn’t whether Nvidia beats its buyers by February. Nobody knows that, and a long-run investor doesn’t need to. The question is what price you’d be glad to own it at if the spending keeps rising, and how much of your money should ride on it if it doesn’t. Two dates bring new data: Nvidia’s report on Nov 17, and the four buyers’ 2027 spending plans in late January and early February. Neither is a reason to trade. Both are reasons to check your plan. For reference, Thursday’s close: Nvidia $181.60, Amazon $260.21, Microsoft $535.93, Alphabet $282.57, Meta $605.08. Further than you’d like. In our look at how low AI chip stocks could go, a drop the size of chip stocks’ 2022 fall would put Nvidia near $129, about 29% below Thursday’s close. Three things could get it there: The next test comes sooner: Nvidia reports its quarter on Nov 17. 1. Decide your price before you decide yes or no. If you’d only want Nvidia meaningfully cheaper than $182, say how much cheaper and write it down now, not after the next 10% move. 2. Get paid to wait for it. One example, for education only: a cash-secured put at a $170 strike expiring May 21, 2027, about six months out, paid about $16.90 a share at Thursday’s close (midpoint of the bid and ask), an effective entry near $153, about 16% below Thursday’s close. Per contract you set aside $17,000 and collect about $1,690. The risk: if Nvidia falls to our $129 worst case, you still buy at $170, about $2,400 per contract worse than buying at that low, after the premium. 3. Count what you already own. An S&P 500 fund already holds Nvidia and all four of its buyers, worth about $16 trillion together. If adding Nvidia takes your AI share past your target, skip step 2. This is education, not personal advice; options aren’t right for every account. We call it Exposure hides in plain sight. A buyer’s spending is its supplier’s revenue. On Wednesday the market bought Amazon and Alphabet for spending less and sold Nvidia for the same reason, and an index fund owned both sides of that bet. Before you buy a dip, ask what has to be true for it to be a dip and not a new, lower price. Here it’s one thing: the four keep spending. You’ll know in February. Nvidia at $182 is a reasonable price, not an obvious bargain. It trades at about 23 times earnings, below Microsoft, and makes twice the free cash flow of its four biggest buyers combined. Wednesday priced in spending cuts that Alphabet and Amazon say aren’t coming. Don’t chase it and don’t dump it: decide your price below $182, keep your AI share inside your band, and let Nvidia’s report and the February spending plans tell you whether to revisit the plan. Follow this story with us: after Nvidia’s report and the February spending plans, we’ll come back with what changed for a long-run holder, and what didn’t. Elections change the odds, not your plan. title: Nvidia Stock (NVDA) Falls 9.3% as AI Chip Stocks Slide (Nov 5) - Gotrade
content: Gotrade News - In the latest Nvidia stock news, shares of Nvidia (NVDA) fell 9.26% to close at $181.60 on Thursday, November 5, 2026, as a broad sell-off in AI and chip stocks deepened. Nvidia stock lost $18.53 in the session, and financial media tied the drop to election-related uncertainty and worries about data center demand rather than company-specific news. Regular-session close on Thursday, November 5, 2026, 4:00 p.m. New York time. Stock prices: Yahoo Finance, cross-checked against the closing price on Nasdaq.com. Volume and 30-day average volume: Nasdaq.com. 52-week range: Yahoo Finance daily highs and lows since November 6, 2025. Indices and the 10-year Treasury yield: Yahoo Finance daily closes for the same date. Follow NVDA's latest price on our Nvidia (NVDA) stock price today page. Nvidia opened at $196.07, below the previous close of $200.13, and traded between $181.46 and $196.25 as selling built through the day. The stock finished just $0.14 above its intraday low, closing near the bottom of its range. Trading was unusually heavy. Volume reached 306.1 million shares, 191.70% above the average of 104.9 million shares. The decline came on a weak day for the whole market. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315.00, the S&P 500 dropped 4.36% to 7,353.73 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 3.44% to 51,523.06, which left Nvidia 3.74 percentage points behind the Nasdaq. The US 10-year Treasury yield eased 5.7 basis points to 4.84% in the same session. Several chip peers fell harder than Nvidia. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) dropped 17.26% and Micron (MU) lost 17.46%, while Broadcom (AVGO) fell 10.43% and TSMC slid 10.78%. After the session, Nvidia sits 25.38% below its 52-week high of $243.37 and 10.55% above its 52-week low of $164.27. None of the reports on the session named a company-specific cause for Nvidia's drop. According to The Motley Fool, investors were selling AI and chip names on November 5 as election-related uncertainty and demand worries intensified, and the move reflected skepticism about demand and policy uncertainty rather than company news. title: NVDA Stock Faces the Last Support as Midterm Elections Put Data-Centre Spending and Nvidia Under Pressure - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) stock has fallen below $200 to around $181, extending their retreat from record highs above $243 as Democratic victories in the US midterm elections intensify concerns about data-centre expansion, electricity shortages, financing costs and growing political opposition to the technology infrastructure boom. Nvidia shares have suffered another sharp reversal after failing to sustain their recover. The stock initially rebounded towards $210 last week, supported by improving geopolitical sentiment, but renewed selling pressure has pushed shares down to approximately $181. The latest decline reflects growing concerns about the enormous infrastructure commitments underpinning semiconductor valuations. Investors are increasingly questioning whether technology companies can maintain their current investment pace as financing costs rise, electricity availability becomes more challenging and political resistance to new data centers gains momentum. Nvidia has now retreated significantly from its record above $243, with the immediate technical picture deteriorating. The $180 area is the next important support zone, while a decisive break lower could expose further downside towards $150. Buyers would need to reclaim $200 to improve the immediate outlook and restore confidence in a recovery. The Democratic victories in the US midterm elections have introduced a new political risk for Nvidia and the wider semiconductor industry. Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott in Texas, becoming the state’s first Democratic governor in more than three decades. Her campaign included a proposal for an immediate freeze on new data-centre developments. Similar opposition has emerged in Ohio and Georgia, where Governor-elect Amy Acton and Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms have also called for greater restrictions on unchecked infrastructure expansion. The election results highlight a broader shift in public sentiment. Reports indicate that 40 of 41 direct votes concerning data-centre projects failed, while several candidates supporting rapid expansion also lost their races. This creates a difficult environment for technology companies that have committed enormous amounts of capital to infrastructure construction. There are several reasons why investors are reassessing the sector: Political opposition: Local communities are increasingly resisting new data centres because of concerns about electricity consumption, water requirements and the impact on household utility bills. Electricity shortages: Power infrastructure may struggle to accommodate the pace of planned construction, potentially delaying projects and reducing the returns on invested capital. Higher construction costs: Companies could be forced to finance additional electricity generation and supporting infrastructure rather than relying entirely on existing power grids. Spending discipline: Investors are beginning to reward technology companies that demonstrate greater capital discipline rather than simply increasing infrastructure budgets. For Nvidia, this is particularly important because its future revenue expectations remain heavily dependent on continued spending by major cloud providers. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $180 today where NVDA is testing the last support at the 100 weekly SMA in yellow. Despite the deteriorating share price, Nvidia continues to expand its influence across the semiconductor supply chain. CEO Jensen Huang’s reported involvement in Marvell Technology’s acquisition of Lumentum Holdings highlights the company’s strategic relationships with infrastructure suppliers. According to Bloomberg, Marvell CEO Matthew Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston consulted Huang before announcing the transaction, which values Lumentum at approximately $115 billion in enterprise value. Nvidia previously invested $2 billion in each company, strengthening its exposure to optical networking and data-centre connectivity. However, the enormous transaction also highlights the capital requirements associated with expanding the infrastructure supporting advanced computing. Not all developments point towards a slowdown. Reports indicate that Anthropic plans to increase its computing capacity beyond 3.5 gigawatts by the end of 2026, potentially reaching approximately 7 gigawatts in 2027. This demonstrates that demand for computing infrastructure remains substantial, providing support for Nvidia’s longer-term growth prospects. Samsung Electronics is also reportedly preparing to manufacture base dies for high-bandwidth memory chips intended for Nvidia and AMD at its second foundry facility in Taylor, Texas. Construction is expected to begin this month, with mass production targeted for 2030. Nevertheless, strong demand projections do not necessarily guarantee that infrastructure projects will be completed on schedule or generate sufficient returns. Competition is another challenge for Nvidia. Google and Oracle have announced plans to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027. This provides customers with another alternative to Nvidia-powered systems as major technology companies attempt to reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers. Nvidia maintains considerable advantages through its established software ecosystem, performance and customer relationships. However, the expansion of custom processors could eventually pressure pricing and market share, even if overall computing demand continues growing. Financing conditions are becoming increasingly important for the semiconductor industry. CoreWeave has experienced significant pressure as yields on its debt maturing in 2032 climbed towards 15%, highlighting the risks associated with heavily leveraged infrastructure expansion. Electricity shortages are also creating deployment problems. Amazon reportedly has Nvidia-equipped server racks waiting in warehouses because some data centres lack sufficient electricity to operate them. Such delays could increase storage costs and postpone revenue generation from infrastructure investments, raising further questions about the returns expected from the current spending cycle. Nvidia remains one of the strongest companies in the semiconductor industry, with substantial customer relationships and exposure to long-term computing demand. However, the market is increasingly questioning whether infrastructure spending can continue expanding at the pace previously anticipated. The Democratic election victories have brought political opposition to data-centre construction into the mainstream, adding to concerns about electricity availability, financing costs and competition. Technically, the decline below $200 represents a significant setback. The $180 level is now critical, with a sustained break potentially opening the door towards $150. A recovery above $200 would be needed to improve the immediate technical picture. For now, sellers remain in control. Despite continued demand for advanced processors, Nvidia shares could remain under pressure as investors demand stronger evidence that the enormous infrastructure investments supporting current valuations will generate sustainable returns.

title: Nvidia Stock To $129? - Trefis
content: Part of our AI selloff guide. Start here: what the Nasdaq correction means for your money. Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. The Nasdaq 100 closed Monday more than 10% below its Oct 6 peak, which is the textbook definition of a correction. The worst day was Friday, Oct 30, when chip stocks (the iShares Semiconductor ETF) fell about 8% after Amazon’s and Alphabet’s results and a weak profit forecast from Intel. By Wednesday the index had bounced to about 9% below its peak, but chip stocks fell another 3% that day. The fear behind the selloff is simple: JPMorgan expects about $900 billion of AI spending worldwide in 2026, and investors want to know when that money pays back. The stock at the center of AI spending is down the least. The deepest falls are company-specific or come after the biggest run-ups. If this were purely a vote against AI spending, Nvidia, the biggest chip company and the one most tied to that spending, should be leading the way down. It isn’t. Intel lost more than a third of its value in five days after its own forecast. Micron and Dell are down hard, but both had more than doubled over the past year. 12-month price changes to Nov 4: Micron +265%, Dell +141%, AMD +95%, Marvell +82%, Intel +57%, Nvidia +1%, Broadcom −8%, Super Micro −38%. Prices are the Wed Nov 4 close (Trefis market data). AMD closed Tue Nov 3, before its report, at $483.90. “Below 52-week high” is how far each stock sits under its highest close of the past year. A stock that more than doubled can fall 30% and still be up on the year; Micron is the clearest case. Company-specific. Intel fell on its own weak profit forecast, not on anyone’s AI budget. Its 39% five-day drop is the biggest in the table. Super Micro has been falling for a year (−38% over 12 months) for reasons that started before this selloff. The payoff doubt. Memory (Micron), networking and optical chips (Marvell) and the companies that build AI servers (Dell, Super Micro) all sold off together after the big cloud companies reported. These businesses get paid first when data centers are built, so they’re the first to be marked down when investors worry that building slows. Marvell’s 36% five-day drop is the biggest of that group. Nvidia and Broadcom sit in between. They are the biggest chip companies selling into AI spending, but they’ve held up best over the past five days (−7% each). That tells you the market isn’t yet betting that the spending stops. It’s betting that the spending gets more careful, and that the suppliers with the thinnest edge get squeezed first. A lot further than this, usually. From late 2021 to late 2022, chip stocks (the iShares Semiconductor ETF) fell about 46% from their peak, and Nvidia fell about 66%. In late 2018, Nvidia lost more than half its value in about three months. In the 2000–2002 bust, many chip stocks fell by more than 80%: Intel about 82%, AMD about 93%. And it’s not only chips: Meta fell about 77% from its 2021 peak to its 2022 low, and it stayed profitable throughout. Here’s what a 2022-sized fall (46% from the 52-week high) would mean for each stock today: The 52-week highs are each stock’s highest close of the past year. For Nvidia, a repeat of its own 2022 fall (−66%) would mean about $81 a share. That’s the outer edge, not a forecast. In 2022, the Fed was raising interest rates fast, from near zero to above 4%. That isn’t the main story today. Here’s what this table means at home: if you own broad index funds, you own every one of these stocks, often on top of the ones you bought yourself. Chip stocks have fallen 46% to 66% before, in less than a year. If you have $1 million or more invested, a Trefis partner firm can show you how much of your portfolio rides on one industry. That the slowdown investors fear hasn’t reached AMD’s order book. It reported after the close on Tuesday, Nov 3: third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45%, against about $13.1 billion expected, and record data center revenue of $8.5 billion, up 97%. The number that mattered was the fourth-quarter guide: about $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, against the roughly $16.3 billion analysts expected. CEO Lisa Su added that she expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027. AMD closed Tuesday at $483.90, before the report, 25% below its 52-week high. After rising more than 4% in early trading Wednesday, it closed up only 1.0%, at $488.78, while Nvidia fell 3.2%. The market took it as good news for AMD, not yet as an all-clear for the group: AMD can grow by taking share even if total AI spending slows, and Nvidia, already far bigger than AMD, has less room to do that. What AMD’s guidance says about the slide, and whether the drop was overdone. Nvidia reports on Tuesday, Nov 17. It guided this quarter’s revenue to about $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. Nvidia is the real test of the payoff question because its customers are the companies doing much of that $900 billion of spending. If its outlook for next quarter keeps rising, the selloff in suppliers looks like a scare. If it flattens, the 2022 yardstick starts to apply to Nvidia too. Two of the eight have already fallen as far as chip stocks did in 2022; Nvidia has fallen about a third of that far. The worst drops of the past five days are Intel’s own forecast and a reset in the suppliers that had run furthest. AMD’s beat-and-raise on Tuesday says its customers are still buying; whether the whole group avoids a 2022-style reset now rides on Nvidia’s report in about two weeks.
